doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Trio, swing and the piano players
title: Swinging versus playing with the time; Oscar Peterson and quotes from Frishberg and Redman
summary: Rowe says swing has become square. Pizzarelli talks about finding pianists who swing, Oscar Peterson, and reads quotes from Frishberg and Joshua Redman on the swinging blues.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Like dropping the mic I guess. Something you just said made me think of — I’m not, I haven’t kept up as much as I should on current instrumental jazz releases but when I listen these days it almost seems like swinging — to swing — has become square. And nobody wants to just play the time, they all want to play with the time.

Well you know I had this conversation with Isaiah. And I was saying you know I get lucky because I manage to find piano players who want to swing, who want to play tunes, and participate in the band like that. I’ve heard — I mean I’ve been in bands where I’m the guy who’s trying to play rhythm guitar and the group is a completely different animal and the rhythm guitar is a dinosaur and you sort of just go oh, I’m fighting the wrong fight here. And so I’m amazed that I can find piano players who want to play tunes and Isaiah’s like this — Isaiah actually made a point about — there was an Oscar Peterson tribute at Lincoln Center or something and he went and he said it was like nobody was there, it was sort of like — it’s almost taken for granted, for Oscar Peterson especially, I’ve talked about it over the years is that you know the most swinging piano player, one of the swingingest piano players on the planet — one of the swingingest musicians. There’s so much to learn from him and it’s sort of like yeah, yeah, well he was swinging. You know they’re swinging. Well I always say there are certain tunes, because “I Know That You Know,” that song. D 7, G 7, C, A 7. D 7, G 7, C [scats]. You know if you’re going [scats] you know we could try and play that altogether. I’ve been playing that song, I mean that’s sort of the litmus test for me, these kinds of — I actually have, I keep it in my phone, if this is okay with you.

This — I have these quotes that I like to — I call it Random Quotes. One in particular, just so you know what I keep in here, it’s something Dave Frishberg said. He said, “Jazz musicians were hip. They were funny, they were sensitive, they were clannish, and they seemed to have the best girlfriends.” That’s something Dave Frishberg — just so you know what I have in here. But I have this quote from Joshua Redman. And I read it to Isaiah one night and he was like, “Can you send that to me?” And so he said, “I still think one of the hardest things to do is to get up there and just play a medium tempo swinging blues. Just to swing with focus, with power, and with relaxation. That’s an incredibly difficult thing to do. There may be some musicians who, to be quite honest, can’t do it and don’t want to spend the time learning how to do it, so they justify that by saying okay, this is not modern. But some of the more modern jazz musicians, even if they

aren’t playing music that is technically swing music, the ones that are good have dealt with that and have that as a basis in what they do. And if they want up on the bandstand on a jam session and the band was playing ‘C Jam Blues’ they could get up there and take a smoking solo on that.” And I think that’s the best explanation. You know so you have the knowledge of it at least. It’s not an excuse to say, “Oh I’m not going to do that.” I hope that made some sense.
